summary: This informational document shows how Segment Routing can solve the BGP Egress Peer Engineering requirement. In this design a centralized SDN controller can program any egress peer policy at ingress border routers or at hosts within the domain.

eli5.summary: A traffic controller can decide which exit road cars take out of a city and tell the entrance gates. This document shows how to do that with Segment Routing.

subtitle: Using Segment Routing to give a central controller the ability to steer traffic out of a network through specific exit points and peers.

tldr.problem: In a large network, an operator might want a central controller to decide which exit peer (external neighbor) traffic should use for a particular destination. BGP normally picks the best path automatically, leaving no room for centralized override. A solution is needed that lets the controller program these policies without updating every border router individually.
tldr.mechanism: Segment Routing (SR) assigns segment IDs to BGP peers at the egress border router and advertises them via BGP-LS. A central SDN controller collects topology and policies, decides which exit to use, and programs the ingress router with a segment list that directs traffic to the chosen egress and peer.
tldr.outcome: Network operators can centrally steer traffic to specific peers for load balancing, business policies, or SLA requirements. The solution works without per-route labels and integrates into existing BGP infrastructures.

today: RFC 9087 is Informational and describes an architecture for centralized BGP egress peer engineering using Segment Routing. The RFC specifies how to allocate and advertise BGP Peering SIDs and how a controller uses them to program policies. RFC 9086 defines the BGP-LS extensions for signaling these SIDs.

sections.title: The BGP-EPE Problem
sections.content:
BGP Egress Peer Engineering (BGP-EPE) lets a centralized controller choose which exit peer (external BGP neighbor) a network uses to reach a particular destination. Normally, BGP on each border router independently selects the best path to a destination based on its own routing information. A centralized controller has no way to override this choice without modifying each router's configuration.

The challenge is to provide the controller with a way to steer traffic to non-best-path peers for business reasons: perhaps to balance load, meet SLA requirements with specific peers, follow customer contracts, or respond to real-time traffic conditions. A network operator should be able to program such policies at border routers or even at source hosts within the domain, not just rely on automatic BGP selection.

This RFC shows how Segment Routing solves this problem. Instead of per-route label allocation, SR defines segments that represent peers, and the controller uses these segments to steer traffic.
sections.eli5: A network operator wants to tell traffic which exit door to use when leaving the network to reach the internet. Normally, each router decides on its own using BGP. This shows how a central controller can override those decisions.

sections.title: BGP Peering Segment Types
sections.content:
A border router allocates three types of BGP Peering Segments (SIDs) to represent paths to external peers.

PeerNode SID represents an entire peer node (an external autonomous system neighbor). Traffic with this SID is load-balanced across all links to that peer. For example, SID 1052 might mean "reach peer F," and traffic with this SID is sent to any available interface to F.

PeerAdj SID represents a specific link (adjacency) to a peer. This is used when a border router has multiple physical links to the same peer and the controller wants to choose a specific link. For example, SID 1032 might mean "use the upper link to F" and SID 1042 "use the lower link to F."

PeerSet SID represents a set of peers that belong together, such as all peers in a particular external AS. Traffic sent to a PeerSet SID is load-balanced across all members of the set.

The RFC specifies how each border router allocates these SIDs to its own peers and advertises them via BGP-LS to the central controller.
sections.eli5: A router puts labels on its exit doors: one label for each neighbor, one for each specific cable to a neighbor that has multiple cables, and one for a group of neighbors. The controller can pick any label to choose where traffic goes.

sections.title: The BGP-EPE Controller
sections.content:
A central BGP-EPE controller collects information from border routers and decides on policies. The controller gathers: BGP paths from all peers (which destinations are reachable via which peers), internal topology (the structure of the network), external topology (the BGP peering segments advertised by border routers via BGP-LS), SLA characteristics of each peer (latency, loss, throughput), traffic matrix (where traffic is flowing), and business policies (contract requirements, load balancing rules).

On the basis of this information, the controller decides which peer to use for which traffic. It expresses this decision as a BGP-EPE policy: typically a segment list with two elements. The first element is the node SID of the chosen egress border router. The second element is a BGP peering SID at that router, specifying the chosen peer or link.

The controller then programs this segment list at ingress border routers or source hosts. When traffic matches a policy, it is steered with the segment list, ensuring it uses the chosen peer.
sections.eli5: A central computer collects information about which neighbors have which paths, how fast they are, how much traffic flows through them, and business rules. It then decides "traffic to destination X should go through peer Y" and tells the entrance routers.

sections.title: Implementing Policies
sections.content:
The controller implements BGP-EPE policies at ingress border routers or at source hosts within the domain. At an ingress router, the policy is typically a traffic-engineering tunnel or a route policy that prepends the segment list. At a source host (like a content server), the host itself can insert the segment list into outgoing packets if the host supports segment routing.

Examples of policies the RFC describes: {64, 1012} means "reach router C (SID 64) via peer AS 2 (PeerNode SID 1012)," {64, 1022} means "reach C via peer E," {64, 1052} means "reach C via peer F." For specific links, {64, 1042} means "reach C via the lower link to F." For peer sets, {64, 1060} means "reach C via any peer in the set E and F."

The segment list can be extended with additional segments for explicit path engineering within the domain. This enables the controller to steer traffic not just to an egress peer but along a chosen path within the network to that peer.
sections.eli5: The controller tells routers: "When you see traffic destined for X, prepend these directions (segments) so the packet reaches the router we chose and exits through the peer we picked."
